explicacion.en: Because ¿te parece bien que…? takes the subjunctive, learners often use the subjunctive after si as well. After ¿te parece si…? the verb stays in the ordinary present: vamos, salimos, nos vemos.
After ¿te parece bien que…? the verb goes in the present subjunctive: comamos, not comemos. It is the opposite of ¿te parece si…?, which takes the plain present.
In English you can drop “that” (“Is it OK we eat there?”). Spanish cannot drop que: ¿Te parece bien que comamos allí?
This is a word-for-word copy of “It seems good to me.” Spanish uses me / te / le / les before parece, like gustar: Me parece bien.

texto.en: To suggest a plan and ask what the other person thinks, Spanish uses the verb parecer, to seem. There are two patterns. First: ¿Te parece si + present? This is like “How about we…?”. After si the verb is in the ordinary present, not the subjunctive: ¿Te parece si salimos a las siete? Second: ¿Te parece bien que + present subjunctive? This is like “Is it OK with you if…?”. The word que is required, and the verb after it is in the subjunctive: ¿Te parece bien que vayamos en bus? ¿Te parece bien que Daniela venga? A quick rule: si takes the present, bien que takes the subjunctive. Parecer works like gustar: te, le and les show who is being asked. The thing being proposed is what “seems” good.

To accept you can say Me parece bien (It sounds good to me) or Me parece perfecto (It sounds perfect to me). To decline politely, say Mejor no, gracias (Better not, thanks). To make a counter-suggestion, use ¿Qué tal si…? (What about if…?) or ¿Y si…? (What if…?) plus the present: ¿Qué tal si nos vemos en la terminal? With a friend like Mateo or Daniela, use te: ¿Te parece si…? With a person you address as usted, use le: ¿Le parece bien que paremos en el banco? With several people (ustedes), use les: ¿Les parece si salimos a las siete? Emma uses usted with a taxi driver and tú with Mateo and Daniela.
You already know these forms from lessons 2–4 and 15. Use them after ¿te parece bien que…? Tap each form to hear it. Nosotros here means “let's” as well: vayamos = let's go.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Si lloverá, nos quedaremos en casa.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Si llueve, nos quedaremos en casa.

explicacion.en: After si, Spanish uses the present even when you mean the future: Si llueve, not “si lloverá”. The future goes only in the result part: nos quedaremos.
The same rule applies to every verb: si tengo, not “si tendré”. Use the present after si and the future in the other half.
After si you need a conjugated verb, not the infinitive. English “If I have time” becomes si tengo tiempo.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Nos quedamos en casa, sí llueve.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Nos quedamos en casa si llueve.

explicacion.en: Si (if) has no accent mark. Sí with an accent means yes. Also, with the si-part at the end you do not need a comma.

texto.en: To talk about something that may really happen, use si (if) + the present tense, then say the result. The present after si can refer to the future: Si llueve, iremos a un café means “If it rains, we'll go to a café.” Never put the future after si: you say si llueve, not “si lloverá”. English works the same way (“If it rains”, not “If it will rain”), so this should feel familiar. The result can be in the future (Si llueve, iremos a un café), in the present, which is very common in speech (Si llueve, nos quedamos en casa), or a command (Si llueve, lleva un paraguas). The si-part can also go last, with no comma: Nos quedamos en casa si llueve.

A plan A and a plan B are two si-sentences: one for the good case and one for the bad case. Si no llueve, saldremos a las siete. Si llueve, iremos a un café. Use si no + present for the negative case: si no llueve means “if it doesn't rain”. Weather verbs are always in the él form: llueve, hace frío, hay neblina. Notice that the si-part and the result part have different subjects and verbs, and each one is conjugated on its own: Si Mateo puede, vendrá con nosotros.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Cuando llegas a la terminal, llámame.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Cuando llegues a la terminal, llámame.

explicacion.en: In English you say “When you arrive” with the plain present, so learners keep the plain present in Spanish. For an action that has not happened yet, Spanish needs the subjunctive after cuando: llegues.
As with si, the future does not go right after cuando. Use the present subjunctive: venga. The future goes only in the other half: saldremos.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Cuando llego a Mindo, te llamaré.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Cuando llegue a Mindo, te llamaré.

explicacion.en: The action has not happened yet, so you need the subjunctive. For -ar verbs the endings use e: llegue, llegues, llegue, lleguemos, lleguen. Note the spelling: g becomes gu before e.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Cuando llueva, me quedo en casa.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Cuando llueve, me quedo en casa.

explicacion.en: For a habit or a general fact (every time it rains), use the plain present after cuando: llueve. The subjunctive is only for one future action that has not happened yet.

texto.en: Cuando means “when”. When it talks about an action that has not happened yet, the verb after cuando goes in the present subjunctive: Cuando llegues, llámame (When you arrive, call me). English uses the plain present here (“When you arrive”), so Spanish needs the extra step. The other half of the sentence can be a future (Cuando lleguemos, comeremos), a present (Cuando llegue Mateo, salimos) or a command (Cuando llegues, llámame). A quick test: has it happened yet? If not, use the subjunctive. If cuando introduces a habit (Cuando llueve, me quedo en casa) or something that already happened (Cuando llegué, llovía), use the indicative. Remember that si + present is different: Si llegas, llámame uses the plain present.

The same pattern works with usted: Cuando llegue a la esquina, gire a la derecha. Both verbs are in the usted form: llegue (subjunctive) and gire (command). With ustedes, use the ellos form: Cuando lleguen a Mindo, llámennos. Emma uses usted with the taxi driver and tú with Daniela and Mateo.
Review of the rule from lessons 2–4: take the yo form of the present, drop the -o, and add the opposite vowel: -e for -ar verbs, -a for -er and -ir verbs. Tap each form to hear it.

explicacion.en: A negative command does not use the affirmative form (llega) with no. It uses the subjunctive: no llegues. Compare: llega (arrive!) but no llegues (don't arrive).
Ve is only for the affirmative: ve (go!). For the negative command, use the subjunctive of ir: no vayas, no vaya, no vayan.
With usted, the negative command uses the subjunctive: no se preocupe. No se preocupa is a plain statement (“he doesn't worry”).
Do not mix the tú pronoun te with the usted ending -e. With tú, use no te preocupes; with usted, no se preocupe.

explicacion.en: In negative commands the pronoun goes before the verb and is written separately: no me llames. In affirmative commands it attaches to the end: llámame.

texto.en: To tell someone tú not to do something, put no before the present subjunctive tú form: no llegues, no olvides, no pierdas, no vayas. This is different from the affirmative command, which uses the plain form: llega, olvida, pierde, ve. For -ar verbs the negative ends in -es (no llegues, no olvides), and for -er and -ir verbs it ends in -as (no pierdas, no comas, no vengas). Contrast the pairs: llega / no llegues; come / no comas; ve / no vayas; ven / no vengas. The pronouns go before the verb and stay separate: no me llames, no lo pierdas, no te apures. Compare the affirmative, where they attach to the end: llámame, espérame.

With usted and ustedes, the negative command uses the same subjunctive form as the affirmative command; only no is added: Llegue temprano / No llegue tarde. Pronouns still go before the verb: No se preocupe, No se olvide de su mochila. With ustedes, use the ellos form: No lleguen tarde, No pierdan los boletos. Many reflexive verbs are used in commands: preocuparse (no se preocupe), apurarse (no te apures), olvidarse de (no se olvide de su mochila). Emma uses usted with the taxi driver and tú with Daniela.
Each row shows the tú command, then the negative commands with tú, usted and ustedes. Tap each form to hear it.

titulo.en: Time limits: hasta que and antes de que

texto.en: Hasta que means “until” and antes de que means “before”. For an action that has not happened yet, both are followed by the present subjunctive: Esperaremos hasta que pare la lluvia (We will wait until the rain stops). Salgamos antes de que llueva más (Let's leave before it rains more). With hasta que, a fact in the past takes the indicative: Esperamos hasta que paró la lluvia (We waited until the rain stopped). Antes de que always takes the subjunctive. If the subject is the same in both parts, use antes de + infinitive and drop que: Antes de salir, llama a Mateo (Before leaving, call Mateo). Compare with cuando: cuando llegues is a moment, hasta que llegues is a limit.

When plans change, you can propose a new date with the pattern from lesson 16: ¿Te parece si lo dejamos para el domingo? (How about we leave it for Sunday?) With several people, use les: ¿Les parece si lo dejamos para el domingo? You can also say Cambiemos el viaje al domingo (Let's change the trip to Sunday). A common way to say “a week from now” is dentro de ocho días: Spanish counts eight days, not seven. Reprogramar and aplazar both mean to reschedule or postpone.
These forms follow hasta que and antes de que. You know most of them from earlier lessons; haya (from haber, the verb behind hay) is the one new form. Tap each form to hear it.

¿Y si lo dejamos para el domingo?

contexto.en: Saturday morning, in the taxi to the terminal. The rain turns into a downpour. Emma and the driver stop under a roof, and Emma calls Daniela, who is on the city bus to the terminal with Mateo. Emma uses usted with the driver and tú with Daniela and Mateo.

dialogo.texto: Señorita, ahora hay un aguacero muy fuerte. ¿Le parece bien que paremos bajo ese techo? Esperamos hasta que pare la lluvia.

traduccion.en: Miss, now there is a very heavy downpour. Is it OK with you if we stop under that roof? We wait until the rain stops.

dialogo.texto: Me parece bien. Yo aguardo aquí con usted. Voy a llamar a Daniela. Hola, Daniela. ¿Dónde estás?

traduccion.en: That sounds fine. I'll wait here with you. I'm going to call Daniela. Hi, Daniela. Where are you?

dialogo.texto: Estamos en el bus para la terminal, Emma. ¡Qué aguacero! Mateo está conmigo.

traduccion.en: We're on the bus to the station, Emma. What a downpour! Mateo is with me.

dialogo.texto: Hola, Mateo. Hay un cambio de planes. ¿Les parece si lo dejamos para el domingo?

traduccion.en: Hi, Mateo. There's a change of plans. How about we leave it for Sunday?

dialogo.texto: Es un cambio de planes, pero me parece bien. ¿Hasta cuándo esperamos hoy?

traduccion.en: It's a change of plans, but it sounds fine to me. Until when do we wait today?

dialogo.texto: Hoy esperamos hasta que pare la lluvia y volvemos a casa. El domingo salimos temprano, antes de que haya tráfico.

traduccion.en: Today we wait until the rain stops and we go back home. On Sunday we leave early, before there is traffic.

dialogo.texto: ¿Y si el domingo tampoco se puede?

traduccion.en: And if Sunday isn't possible either?

dialogo.texto: Entonces miramos la programación del bus y lo reprogramamos para dentro de ocho días.

traduccion.en: Then we look at the bus schedule and reschedule it for a week from now.

dialogo.texto: Perfecto. Aclaro: el domingo salimos a las siete, ¿verdad?

traduccion.en: Perfect. Let me clarify: on Sunday we leave at seven, right?

dialogo.texto: Sí, a las siete. Antes de salir, llámame, Mateo.

traduccion.en: Yes, at seven. Before leaving, call me, Mateo.

dialogo.texto: Gracias, Emma. El domingo, ¿te parece si nos vemos en la terminal a las siete menos diez?

traduccion.en: Thanks, Emma. On Sunday, how about we meet at the terminal at ten to seven?

dialogo.texto: Me parece perfecto. ¡Qué fácil es ponerse de acuerdo con ustedes!

traduccion.en: That sounds perfect to me. How easy it is to come to an agreement with you!

dialogo.texto: Señorita, la lluvia ya es llovizna. Esperamos un poco más.

traduccion.en: Miss, the rain is only drizzle now. We wait a little longer.

dialogo.texto: Perfecto. Gracias, señor. Daniela y Mateo, ¡hasta el domingo!

traduccion.en: Perfect. Thank you, sir. Daniela and Mateo, see you Sunday!

dialogo.texto: ¡Hasta el domingo, Emma!

traduccion.en: See you Sunday, Emma!

items.audio: Lo dejamos para el domingo, ¿te parece?

consigna.en: Writing task (at least 25 words, not scored): the trip changes because of the rain. Write to Mateo and Daniela proposing to postpone it to Sunday, saying until when you will wait today and what to do before leaving, with hasta que and antes de que. Compare with the model.

feedback.en: Model: Hola, Mateo y Daniela. ¿Les parece si dejamos el viaje para el domingo? Hoy esperaremos hasta que pare la lluvia. El domingo saldremos temprano, antes de que haya tráfico.

items.respuesta: Hola, Mateo y Daniela. ¿Les parece si dejamos el viaje para el domingo? Hoy esperaremos hasta que pare la lluvia. El domingo saldremos temprano, antes de que haya tráfico.
